# What to do next: make the next experiment auditable

*Research Loop · As of 2026-10-14*

For a student researcher, a useful next agent experiment begins with a boundary: define what the agent may change, what the comparison may cost, and what evidence will justify keeping its result. Our recommendation, inferred from the supplied research and practitioner accounts, is to delegate a narrow search while keeping final evaluation outside that search’s control. This is a practical protocol, not an experimentally validated package for eliminating false conclusions. <!-- 03-c1 03-c2 03-c3 -->

Start with a measurable bottleneck. In AI Code King’s tutorial, the optimizer may revise only a bug-fixing instruction file ([08:23–08:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=503s)). The underlying model remains unchanged; this is instruction optimization, not weight training ([00:51–01:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=51s)). Periodic Labs’ founders offer a physical-lab counterpart: automate routine bottlenecks in service of useful data, with full autonomy explicitly a non-goal ([podcast, 50:46–51:39](https://www.latent.space/p/periodic)). These examples motivate a scope rule, but the founder testimony supplies no independent validation of physical-lab performance. <!-- 03-c1 -->

Before launching the search, test the measuring apparatus. The tutorial proposes checking that a known broken implementation fails, a reviewed correct patch passes, and a forbidden modification is rejected ([05:27–05:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=327s)). The [oversight study, §8](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28614) supplies the broader rationale: protected evaluation data and criteria should remain outside the producing agent’s control. Read together, the sources suggest separating permission to propose and execute experiments from authority to certify their success. Passing these preliminary checks establishes only that the evaluator handles those cases. <!-- 03-c2 -->

The budget should cover the entire comparison. The tutorial’s proposed baseline and candidate evaluations require 36 coding trials, with 12 more for the final comparison: 48 before optimizer reasoning, setup or rehearsals ([12:26–12:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=746s)). Likewise, the [solar-panel segmentation study, §2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10491) caps each campaign at 24 logged experiments, including its baseline; its one-hour training limit applies to an experiment, not the whole search. Our practical inference is to reserve resources for rejected candidates and final checks before spending on optimization. Otherwise, the most important comparison may be the one you cannot afford. <!-- 03-c3 -->

Decide repeat counts before seeing results. [NanoProteinLM’s authors](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/) report training each candidate with two seeds and retaining it only when its mean gain exceeds the seed-to-seed spread. The segmentation paper acknowledges that its protocol does not estimate single-run variation, limiting confidence in small retained improvements. These are different standards of evidence, not interchangeable demonstrations of reliability. <!-- 03-c4 -->

The tutorial also contains a consequential contradiction. Its fixed-attempt rule is immediately followed by an instruction to keep rerunning until lucky ([08:04–08:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=484s)). Reject the latter instruction: choosing when to stop after inspecting outcomes undermines the declared comparison. The supplied tutorial has no execution logs establishing a gain, so it is useful as a proposed procedure, not a demonstrated improvement. Repetition also cannot repair an objective that measures the wrong outcome. <!-- 03-c4 -->

After selection, freeze the candidate and compare it with the baseline on protected fresh tasks. If final-test feedback informs another revision, reserve new evaluation data; the tutorial correctly identifies the previously held-out tasks as development material once used for tuning ([11:02–11:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=662s)). Confidence should also depend on whether comparisons isolate their claimed mechanism. Segmentation changes coding model alongside GPU class, preventing attribution to hardware alone. The oversight study bundles review decisions, reasons and retained history, so its feedback comparison cannot establish an explanation-specific effect. Our inference is to demand both transfer and cleaner comparisons before adopting broader explanations. <!-- 03-c6 -->

Keep failures as carefully as winners. [Agora, §4.8 and Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094), makes the distinction between an archive and verification concrete: its account lacks evaluator logs and several dependency and data version pins, and its authors did not rerun the winning method. The September report documents an April–May run; the recent evidence is the published account, not a newly executed campaign. Its proposed verification record identifies the target hash, reproduction configuration, evaluator and reproduced value. Those details give another researcher something executable to check. <!-- 03-c5 -->

Failure records need equally precise conditions. Periodic’s founders caution that an unsuccessful synthesis does not establish that the material is impossible to make ([podcast, 56:13–56:30 and 56:33–56:46](https://www.latent.space/p/periodic)). Applied to computational work, our interpretation is to preserve what failed under which configuration, rather than label the approach universally unsuccessful. <!-- 03-c5 -->

For future Research Loop coverage, the evidence that should raise confidence is reproducible transfer, complete search-cost accounting and verification that checks the intended claim. Small held-out sets can remain inconclusive, and detailed archives cannot substitute for independent replication. The sources motivate these requirements from different perspectives; they do not collectively prove that the resulting protocol guarantees trustworthy science. <!-- 03-c2 03-c3 03-c5 03-c6 -->

## References

Editorial dispositions below concern use in piece **03**, not publication approval.

- **Accept — bounded procedure, with correction:** AI Code King, [“My Self Training Claude Code Setup”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I), published 2026-10-11.
